narrative:
The model predicted a 62.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors that together signaled a higher risk of struggling with the bar. The most influential was your class ranking at the end of your third year of law school, which placed you in the third decile. This was noticeably lower than the average ranking of students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second strongest factor and followed the same pattern, landing you in the second decile compared with an average of sixth decile among accepted students. These two academic-standing measures pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 36 worked in the opposite direction. While it is only slightly below the 37.18 average of accepted students, it still provided a modest pull toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the downward pressure from your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way. Your family income, undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time were also far less important to the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
